Fire ants!

It wasn't until we were right underneath the tree that I finally spotted the sloth. It dangled upside down from a branch about three metres above our canoe, the long motorised boat that had brought us all the way up the river from the coast. Now I understood why I hadn't seen it earlier.

'It's green!' I said.

Uncle Dean nodded. 'At certain times of year they get algae - kind of like moss - growing in their fur. Want to get a photo?'

I pulled my new camera out of its waterproof case. It was an early birthday present from my parents, who thought it would come in handy on this trip with my botanist uncle. So far we'd seen caimans, capybaras, freshwater dolphins, giant otters, four kinds of monkey and about a million birds - but this was my first sloth.

I tried to find it on the screen. 'Can we go forwards a bit? There are too many leaves in the way.'

Ravi hauled sideways on the outboard motor. It had a long propeller shaft and was hard to steer.

Bump! The front of the canoe hit a submerged log and began to spin around in the current. Uncle Dean grasped an overhead branch to steady us. But the branch was hollow; it snapped off in his hand. And out of its honeycombed interior came a shower of squirming brown insects.

'Fire ants!' cried Ravi. 'Look out!'

His warning came too late. Already Uncle Dean was covered from head to foot in a blanket of fire ants. Their stings are worse than bees.

Ravi didn't hesitate. Scrambling forward, he grabbed Uncle Dean around the middle, lifted him out of his seat and rolled over the side with a huge, two-man splash.

The Trojan Horse

Kryson crouched low in the shadow of Troy's massive stone walls, silently going over his lines one more time. Everything depended on whether he could convince the Trojans that the Greek army had truly given up their ten-year siege and sailed home at last.

He glanced sideways at the enormous wooden horse the crafty Greeks had built and left standing just outside the city gates. Somewhere inside its huge hollow belly, his fellow soldiers were waiting in the heat and the dark. He didn't envy them.

Eventually a few curious Trojans noticed the strange wooden structure and crept closer to investigate. For the first time in a decade, the Greek camp beyond the walls stood completely empty and silent. Was the war really over? And what exactly was this towering horse supposed to mean? Taking a breath, Kryson stepped out of hiding and began his carefully rehearsed story.

'Please, spare me!' he cried out. 'My own countrymen abandoned me when they sailed for home. They've finally accepted they could never conquer Troy. This horse was built as a gift - an offering to your city's strength, left behind as a token of respect.'

Exhausted after years of war, the Trojans were easily won over by Kryson's dramatic performance. Desperate to believe their enemy had truly given up, they decided to haul the horse inside the city walls as a trophy of their victory.

Not everyone was convinced. A handful of Trojans eyed the strange wooden creature with unease and argued against bringing it inside at all, but their warnings were drowned out by the noise of celebration. Thick ropes were tied to the horse, and crowds of excited citizens pushed forward, each eager for the honour of helping pull it through the gates.

And so, without realising it, the Trojans dragged their own enemy straight into the heart of their city. Once night fell, the hidden soldiers climbed down from inside the horse, threw open the gates, and let in the waiting Greek army. Troy fell that same night. Ever since, the phrase 'wooden horse' has come to describe any gift that looks beguiling but ultimately leads to disaster.

Q & A with Rosa Kade

Q. You are co-writing your new series, Storm Twins, with your friend Devon Lowe. Is it hard to write a book with someone else when you are used to writing on your own? How does co-writing a book work?

A. It's actually been a lot of fun working on the book with Devon. While there are many different ways to co-write books, we've developed a process that basically starts with the two of us working out the story in detail, accompanied by a whiteboard and numerous cups of tea (me) and soy hot chocolate (Devon). After that, we work up a chapter outline in even more detail, sending it back and forth until we're both happy with it. Then I write the first chapter and send it to Devon, who very speedily writes a first draft of the rest of the book. That comes back to me, and I revise and expand upon it, adding in detail and so on. Then I send that back to Devon, who does another revision, and we kick it backwards and forwards for more revisions until it's done. At the end, it's very difficult for either of us to identify even a single sentence that we individually wrote, which is good. It makes it a real co-operative work.

Q. Where did the idea for Storm Twins come from?

A. I had a very basic idea that I described to Devon, who instantly added in some more ideas, and then we added in a lot more, and from there went on to actually develop those basic ideas into a story.

Q. Have you and Devon mapped out the complete Storm Twins series, or are some things left to chance?

A. We've outlined five books in some detail, but, as always, when you come to write them, things change, new and better ideas come along, characters turn out differently than they were envisaged, and so on. That's part of the fun of writing.

After that, we work up a chapter outline in even more detail, sending it back and forth until we're both happy with it. Then I write the first chapter and send it to Devon, who very speedily writes a first draft of the rest of the book. That comes back to me, and I revise and expand upon it, adding in detail and so on. Then I send that back to Devon, who does another revision, and we kick it backwards and forwards for more revisions until it's done. At the end, it's very difficult for either of us to identify even a single sentence that we individually wrote, which is good. It makes it a real co-operative work.

Kit's Cradle

They've taken the cosy bed away
That I made myself with the Shetland shawl,
And set me a hamper of scratchy hay,
By that great black stove in the entrance-hall.

I won't sleep there; I'm resolved on that!
They may think I will, but they little know
There's a soft persistence about a cat
That even a little kitten can show.

I wish I knew what to do but pout,
And spit at the dogs and refuse my tea;
My fur's feeling rough, and I rather doubt
Whether stolen sausage agrees with me.

On the drawing-room sofa they've closed the door,
They've turned me out of the easy-chairs;
I wonder it never struck me before
That they make their beds for themselves up-stairs.

I've found a crib where they won't find me,
Though they're crying 'Kitty!' all over the house.
Hunt for the slipper! And riddle-my-ree!
A cat can keep as still as a mouse.

It's rather unwise perhaps to purr,
But they'll never think of the wardrobe-shelves.
I'm happy in every hair of my fur;
They may keep the hamper and hay themselves.

Juliana Horatia Ewing

How the air became perfect

Earth's air has exactly the right mixture of gases you need to live. How do you think this perfect arrangement came to be?

Let's imagine we could board a timeship and travel back about 2.5 billion years, as life was just beginning to take hold on Earth. Stepping out of the timeship, we see a landscape of bare rock and murky water, with no trees, plants or even soil anywhere. But we don't have time to explore, because in two minutes we would be dead! Why? Because the air has almost no oxygen in it. Not only that, we'd be roasted, because the temperature is so high.

Let's say we're wearing oxygen tanks and heat-protector suits. We walk along and come to an ocean. Fortunately, our suits are equipped for deep-sea diving, and we've brought underwater microscopes to help us see super-tiny things. We dive down to the ocean floor and find a world of strange, microscopic creatures. There are beings with tails that whip them along, and others with rows of little bristles moving like oars. There are creatures with shells and spikes. Mixed into this zoo are some blue-green organisms - the ancestors of plants. Over many millions of years, these tiny, plant-like forms have slowly released oxygen into the water and air. But the air still contains too little oxygen to support any but the smallest, simplest creatures.

Let's get back in the timeship and travel forward several hundred million years. Now when we step outside, things are more interesting. The Earth's crust has been moving, draining oceans and exposing their plant-rich floors. Plants have spread across the land. There are all kinds of plants now, and they're all releasing oxygen into the air. We can take off our oxygen masks and just breathe. Because the temperature is cooler now, we can also take off our heat-protector suits.

We can see animals too. They breathe in oxygen and breathe out carbon dioxide. The plants take in carbon dioxide and release oxygen. What a great, harmonious system!

Let's get back in the timeship for our last trip, forward to our own time. Now we see a vast array of different plants and trees, still taking in carbon dioxide and supplying the air with oxygen. Billions of years ago, their ancestors changed the Earth's air by sending oxygen into it. By doing so, they created the essential conditions for life in all its glorious forms.

Lost

Panting, I stared through the mass of purple blooms hanging from the curving branches of the trees like crystals on a chandelier. The petals trembled in the cool wind curling unseen along the riverbank. I felt strangely energetic - nerves, fear, yearning - all tangled together inside my head.

I stepped down the bank carefully, the pebbles slipping under my bare feet. I knew she was there somewhere. I could hear her faint cries, sounds so small, as though someone was playing a piano very softly so as not to wake anyone.

The bank was steep, my movement slow. When I reached the river I stood still, my toes under the surface of the cold, bubbling water. I stretched them out like the fingers of a hand, pushing them into the chocolatey mud and thick strands of weed, and listened for the tiny bleating. Where was she?

I knew this part of the river well. It was where I would come and read when I wanted to get away from home. Here by the river, my back against a tree, my eyes fixed on black printed words, I could sit peacefully, surrounded by a natural world that didn't care who I was at all. Ironically, this lack of concern comforted me. Home was not like that. At home I gasped for breath through the smog of raised voices, banging doors, running feet, the screaming kettle, the arguments, even the laughter.

Down by the river there was none of that. There was only music - ordered, melancholy music - where each instrument took its part and chimed or plucked or sang, without conflict or even emotion. Croaking, piping, humming, hooting, rustling, rippling, splashing - if there were any struggles out here by the river, I couldn't tell. But now, as I stood listening for the little lost creature, I wondered.

Blood for dinner

There are three species of bats that survive entirely by feeding on blood: the common vampire bat, the hairy-legged vampire bat and the white-winged vampire bat. Don't worry, though - all three species are native to the Americas, so you won't find them creeping up on you in the middle of the night as you sleep safely in your bed.

When a vampire bat wakes up and emerges from its dark cave, it hunts for warm-blooded prey, usually sleeping cattle or horses. Once it finds a meal, the bat flies down and lands quietly near the unsuspecting animal, creeping towards it using its legs and wing-covered arms. Using heat sensors on its nose, the bat locates where blood is flowing close to the skin. If the victim is particularly hairy, the vampire bat uses its teeth to shave away the fur. The bat then uses its razor-sharp incisors to slice a small, precise cut, and once blood is freely seeping from its victim, it begins lapping it up.

The vampire bat is well adapted to this liquid diet. Its saliva contains a chemical that stops the prey's blood from clotting as it flows out of the wound, as well as compounds that prevent blood vessels near the wound from tightening, so the blood keeps flowing for the bat to drink.

The vampire bat's digestive system processes its meal so quickly that it can start excreting urine within minutes of feeding. This is necessary because a vampire bat weighs only about 40 grams but can drink more than 20 grams of blood in one sitting - so it must lose some of that weight quickly if it wants to be light enough to fly back to its cave. The trick is to rapidly get rid of the blood plasma, which has no nutritional value. The stomach lining rapidly absorbs the plasma, which is then transported to the kidneys and bladder. Within minutes, the bat is excreting plasma-rich urine and losing enough weight to launch itself back into the night sky.

This blood-feeding habit is called hematophagy, and it isn't limited to vampire bats - certain species of leeches, fish and worms also feed this way.
